- [2023/05/22] Section 7 defines "covered joint resolution" as a joint resolution of disapproval of designation or removal of designation by the Secretary of Commerce.
- [2023/05/22] A joint resolution of disapproval of designation must include specific language stating Congress's disapproval and that such designation shall have no force until evidence is provided to relevant committees.
- [2023/05/22] A joint resolution of disapproval of removal of designation similarly requires specific wording, prohibiting the removal of designation until evidence is presented.
- [2023/05/22] If a foreign government or regime is designated as an adversary, a joint resolution can be introduced within 60 days for expedited consideration.
- [2023/05/22] In the House, if a committee fails to report a covered joint resolution within 10 legislative days, it must be discharged and proceed to floor consideration.
- [2023/05/22] The House allows two hours of debate on a covered joint resolution, equally divided between sponsors and opponents.
- [2023/05/22] In the Senate, a covered joint resolution is referred to relevant committees but must be discharged if not reported within 10 session days.
- [2023/05/22] The Senate allows up to 10 hours of debate on a covered joint resolution, divided equally between majority and minority leaders or their designees.
- [2023/05/22] If one House receives a covered joint resolution from the other before passing its own, it follows the same procedures as if no such resolution had been received.
- [2023/05/22] Section 7 is enacted by Congress as an exercise of rulemaking power for both Houses but does not override existing rules unless inconsistent with them.
- [2023/05/22] A joint resolution of disapproval of designation, if enacted, removes the foreign adversary designation for a specified entity.
- [2023/05/22] A joint resolution of disapproval of removal of designation prevents the removal of an existing foreign adversary designation.
